definition: A profile of how supply, demand, storage, and pipeline connectivity shape the Midwest U.S. natural gas market.
core_idea: Midwest gas demand is driven almost entirely by winter residential heating because coal, not gas, dominates regional power generation, and heavy storage infrastructure with government-mandated winter delivery obligations backstops that seasonal demand.
key_points: Demand is strongly seasonal (winter heating) rather than year-round, unlike regions where gas also fuels power plants.
Coal is the primary power-generation fuel in the Midwest, so summer gas demand is comparatively low.
The region has extensive storage and local distribution networks, and some jurisdictions can compel storage operators to release gas to residential customers ahead of commercial use during winter.
Large pipelines link the Midwest mainly to Canadian and Rocky Mountain supply basins, with supplemental Gulf Coast gas when available.
Midwest basis prices track NYMEX (Henry Hub) futures only loosely, reflecting import access from multiple supply sources.
relationships: Regional power-generation fuel mix determines whether gas demand is seasonal-only or year-round.
trading_implications: Government-mandated winter release obligations can effectively withdraw storage gas from the commercial market at the coldest, highest-demand times.
Looser correlation to Henry Hub implies basis trades here carry more idiosyncratic (supply-source-driven) risk than in tightly correlated regions.
caveats: One might assume gas demand tracks power demand everywhere; in the Midwest it does not, because coal supplies most power generation.
